topic: Why we only see one side of the Moon
claim: The Moon spins once per orbit (tidal locking), so the same face always points at Earth; the far side is not dark, and was first imaged in 1959.

beats.caption: You've never seen half the Moon
beats.vo: You have never seen half the Moon.

beats.caption: Spin = orbit = 27 days
beats.vo: The Moon spins once every 27 days. It also circles Earth once every 27 days. The two match exactly, so the same face always points at us.

beats.caption: Earth's gravity slowed the spin
beats.vo: That match is called tidal locking. Long ago, Earth's gravity stretched the Moon into a football shape. The bulge lagged behind as the Moon spun, and gravity's tug slowed the spin until it matched the orbit.

beats.caption: The far side isn't dark
beats.vo: People call the hidden side the dark side, but it gets sunlight too. At new moon, it is fully lit. We first saw it in 1959, from a Soviet spacecraft. Next new moon, remember: the far side is in full sunshine.

sources.text: NASA Science, Moon Facts: https://science.nasa.gov/moon/facts/ (tidally locked; spins and orbits in 27 Earth days; far side is not 'dark'; new moon = far side fully sunlit; far side first seen 1959 by a Soviet spacecraft)
NASA Science, Tidal Locking: https://science.nasa.gov/moon/tidal-locking/ (Earth's gravity distorted the Moon into a football shape; lagging bulge slowed its spin until it matched its orbit)
NASA Goddard/ASU LROC, The Far Side of the Moon: farside first imaged in 1959 by the Soviet Luna 3 spacecraft
